title: Short Stuff: The Killing Stone
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Sessho-seki (Killing Stone), a volcanic-area boulder on Mount Nasu in Tochigi Prefecture, Japan, which split in two in 2022 and went viral online. Josh and Chuck explain the folklore of Tamamo no Mae, a nine-tailed fox spirit who allegedly seduced Emperor Toba (reigned 1107-1123, per the hosts' dates of 1103-1156 CE life span), was hunted down by samurai after a soothsayer identified her, and whose body turned into the stone. They link the tale to the Hogen Rebellion as an allegory for the rise of samurai rule, note the possible sulfuric gases that seep from the ground, discuss how her depiction evolved into a proto-feminist anti-hero, and describe the stone-focused tourism to the site.

segments.title: Opening and viral tweet
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Killing Stone in Japan, which split in two in 2022, and quote a viral tweet by a tourist who visited the rock.

segments.title: Tamamo no Mae legend and Emperor Toba
segments.summary: The tweeter's visit raised the idea that the fox spirit Tamamo no Mae had escaped the rock. Josh and Chuck explain the folklore: the fox spirit appeared as a woman to seduce Emperor Toba, the emperor's reign, and the legend that she was trapped in a stone.

segments.title: Samurai hunt and Hogen Rebellion allegory
segments.summary: A soothsayer identified the fox spirit, who fled to Mount Nasu, where samurai shot and killed her and her body turned to stone. Folklorists see the story as an allegory for the Hogen Rebellion and the rise of samurai rule.

segments.title: Folklore as political metaphor
segments.summary: Chuck notes that many Japanese folklore stories follow monsters and heroes and often serve as metaphors for political events.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the description of the stone.

segments.title: The stone and Mount Nasu setting
segments.summary: The stone is described as about six feet tall and roughly twenty-five feet around, standing out from others on Mount Nasu, a volcanic plateau with active volcanoes and gas vents that make the area look menacing.

segments.title: Volcanic gases and the 2022 split
segments.summary: Chuck explains that sulfuric gases seep from the ground near the stone, which are not harmful to humans but could seem ominous. He describes how the Internet speculated about the evil spirit being unleashed after the split, while locals do not believe it.

segments.title: Evolving depiction and tourism
segments.summary: Tamamo no Mae was originally portrayed as purely evil and later evolved into a proto-feminist anti-hero in manga and anime. The hosts discuss the stone as a popular tourist attraction in a national park.

segments.title: Content-based tourism
segments.summary: Josh mentions the term content-based tourism for visiting a single attraction, and the hosts banter about the squirrels and the park.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing banter and the iHeartRadio credit.
